rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Adding vectors is the same as adding numbers — Vectors have direction, so you cannot simply add magnitudes unless they point in the same direction. Two 5 N forces at 120° give a resultant of only 5 N, not 10 N.  ·  The resultant is always larger than either component — The resultant can be smaller than one or both components. For opposite directions, $R = |P - Q|$; if $P = Q$, the resultant is zero.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: You can add vectors pointing in different directions by just adding their magnitudes — You must use the parallelogram law, triangle law, or component method. The magnitude of the resultant depends critically on the angle between the vectors.  ·  If the resultant is zero, the vectors must be zero — Two non-zero vectors can have a zero resultant if they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction ($\vec{P} + (-\vec{P}) = \vec{0}$).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The parallelogram law of vector addition was first clearly stated by **Simon Stevin** (1548–1620) in his treatise on statics. He showed that two forces acting at a point are equivalent to a single force represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram.  ·  NEB exam priority: addition of collinear vectors (same/opposite direction) is a guaranteed question type. Master the sign convention: assign one direction as positive, the opposite as negative, then add algebraically.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Case 1 — same direction**: when two vectors $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ point in exactly the same direction ($\theta = 0°$), their resultant has maximum magnitude: $\vec{R} = \vec{P} + \vec{Q}$ with $R = P + Q$. The direction is the same as both original vectors.  ·  **Case 2 — opposite direction**: when $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ point in exactly opposite directions ($\theta = 180°$), the resultant is $\vec{R} = \vec{P} - \vec{Q}$ (assuming $P > Q$) with magnitude $R = |P - Q|$, acting along the direction of the larger vector.  ·  **General formula** (parallelogram/triangle law): for any angle $\theta$ between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$: $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$ and the direction $\alpha$ from $\vec{P}$ is $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Resolution of vectors; unit vectors and other topics  ·  Key Formula 5: Important relation in Resolution of vectors; unit vectors  ·  The angle in the formula is the angle between the tails of the vectors — In the formula $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$, $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors when placed tail-to-tail. If given the exterior angle, use $180° - \text{angle}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Vector addition is not commutative — Vector addition IS commutative: $\vec{P} + \vec{Q} = \vec{Q} + \vec{P}$. What is non-commutative is vector multiplication (cross product): $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} \neq \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$.  ·  A zero resultant means no forces are acting — A zero resultant means all forces balance. Multiple forces can act simultaneously with a net effect of zero (equilibrium).  ·  The direction of the resultant is always between the two vectors — This is true only for $0° < \theta < 180°$. In the special case of opposite vectors ($\theta = 180°$), the resultant lies along the larger vector, not 'between' them.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The difference of two vectors has a larger magnitude than their sum — No. For $0° < \theta < 90°$, $|\vec{P}-\vec{Q}| < |\vec{P}+\vec{Q}|$ because $\cos\theta > 0$. The difference is only larger when $\theta > 90°$.  ·  You can cancel vectors by just writing them with opposite signs — You must be careful about what 'cancels' what. $\vec{P} + (-\vec{P}) = \vec{0}$ only if they act at the same point. If they act at different points (non-concurrent forces), they produce a couple, not cancellation.  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Resolution of vectors; unit vectors
